e.t: This Hebrew word refers to a prison—a place where a person is held in confinement. It functions as a noun naming such a place, rather than describing the act of imprisoning someone. The word occurs 10 times in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, including passages rendered with “prison” in 2 Kings 25:29 and Isaiah 42:7. Its broader use also includes settings where people are confined or kept under restraint, while the surrounding verse determines the particular situation.

This word refers to a place named “Chesalon,” rather than expressing a general action, quality, or object. It functions as a proper place-name in the Hebrew Old Testament and occurs once, in Joshua 15:10. This Hebrew word refers to a “proclamation,” a message announced publicly so that it can be heard and recognized by others. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense centers on an official public announcement.

This Hebrew verb means “bray,” describing the sound an animal makes. Hallohesh is a Hebrew personal name, functioning as the designation of an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. It occurs twice in the Old Testament, both times in Nehemiah. Since it is presented as a name, its meaning for readers is mainly identifying the person associated with it, not expressing a general idea or instruction. The name appears in Nehemiah 3:12 and Nehemiah 10:24.

The name occurs 146 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, from Genesis through Ezekiel. Its repeated association with family lines and tribal inheritance shows that it identifies a continuing ancestral and tribal line rather than describing an action or quality.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “cubits,” a unit used to describe length, height, width, and distance. It functions as a measurement term, especially in descriptions of the ark, tabernacle furnishings, temple structures, boundaries, and other physical spaces. Its exact size is understood through the measuring context, but its ordinary sense is a cubit-length measure.

Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding context, but its ordinary lexical sense is the clothing itself rather than an action or quality. This is a rare Hebrew word in the surviving biblical occurrences.

e.t: This Hebrew noun means “mouse,” the name of a small animal. It occurs six times in the Hebrew Old Testament, appearing in Leviticus, 1 Samuel, and Isaiah. The references indicate that the word is used as a concrete noun for the animal itself rather than as an abstract quality or action. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic lexical sense remains “mouse.”

This Hebrew word describes a person as “poor.” It is used of people who lack material resources or social strength, presenting poverty as a real human condition rather than merely an inward feeling. The word occurs 78 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, so it has a broad presence in laws, wisdom writings, songs, and prophetic passages. Its repeated use keeps attention on people who are poor and therefore vulnerable within human society.

This Hebrew word describes someone who is “prudent”—acting with good judgment and careful awareness. It is used of a person whose conduct shows practical wisdom rather than careless openness. In the Old Testament, it occurs 11 times, especially in Proverbs, where it characterizes a person who responds thoughtfully and does not display every thought. Its use in Genesis and Job also shows that the same word can describe a calculating quality, so the surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis is commendable or unfavorable.

Because the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, the word’s precise role in that list cannot be expanded beyond identifying the Punites as a distinct group.

This Hebrew word means “judge,” referring to the role of one who makes a judgment or decision. It functions as a term identifying a judging authority rather than describing an action in itself. The word occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Job 31:28. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text and passage, but its basic sense is the person or role connected with judging.

The word appears 74 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing a recurring biblical category connected with warfare, victory, and the handling of what was captured. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Hebrew word refers to a watch, especially a designated period of watching during the night. It functions as a noun for a time or interval kept under watch, rather than describing the person who watches. It occurs seven times in the Hebrew Old Testament, including passages that speak of night watches and the passing of a watch. Its normal sense is therefore a division of the night marked by watchfulness.

Its precise significance in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word consistently functions as the person’s name.
